summary: This work introduces two zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC)—the swirling and sliding variants—that periodically remove leakage via anticommuting two-body measurements while preserving code distance to Pauli errors. Numerical simulations reveal that in the experimentally relevant waterfall regime, entropic effects allow the hFC to outperform the same-distance walking surface code despite lacking asymptotic advantages for some noise models.
motivation: Leakage from qubits exiting the computational subspace induces correlated spatiotemporal errors that reduce code thresholds and effective distance, increasingly dominating the error budget as Pauli-error fidelities improve on platforms like superconducting qubits and neutral atoms.
method: Two circuits implementing the P6 hFC with weight-2 check measurements on a honeycomb lattice are designed: the swirling hFC uses late-SWAP leakage-reduction units (LRUs) and requires physical qubit rearrangement between rounds on reconfigurable architectures; the sliding hFC employs both early- and late-SWAP LRUs compatible with fixed square-lattice connectivity. Both achieve zero overhead by leveraging circuit identities to compile SWAPs into syndrome extraction without additional gates, qubits, or depth.
result: Under depolarizing, tailored, skip-gate, and leakage-transport noise models, the hFC reduces qubit lifetime from 8 gates (surface code) to an average of 4 gates. Numerically, the swirling hFC exhibits steeper logical error rate scaling ($\alpha > d/2$) and crossovers to outperform the walking surface code at lower physical error rates in the waterfall regime, despite upper-bound minimum-weight predictions suggesting no asymptotic advantage for some noise models.
